rationale: A wins because it is stricter about what the facts can actually bear. Its best angle, "Deel's AI flags contractor-classification risk across 150 countries — but won't say how accurate it is," is sharp, grounded, and reporter-shaped. B has better commercial instincts in places, but "deciding whether your contractor is legally an employee" and "liability-bearing decisions" overstate a tool that the update only says flags risks and checks exposure. That's how you get a founder into a correction before breakfast.
gaps_in_A: "Deel's new AI compliance tool arrives with the company mid-lawsuit over corporate espionage" is real news, but dangerous client strategy; it may invite a litigation story with the product as garnish.
"a budget question for HR teams' outside counsel" is plausible but speculative without a customer, spend baseline, or proof this replaces legal review.
"Decay: 24hr" on the accuracy-disclosure angle undersells it; black-box compliance AI in 150 countries can hold for a deeper accountability piece.
The first angle needs tighter caution around whether the espionage lawsuit has any connection to compliance data; A asks it later, but the kept angle leans hard before that fact is known.
gaps_in_B: "deciding whether your contractor is legally an employee" overclaims the update; Deel's tool flags risks and checks classification, it is not shown to make binding legal decisions.
"liability-bearing decisions" is unsupported unless B can prove customers rely on the tool as a legal determination and bear consequences from its output.
"betting the feature is worth more as lock-in than as revenue" is an interesting thesis, but it invents pricing strategy from the single fact that the tool is included for existing customers.

Refusing "Deel launches AI compliance tool amid espionage lawsuit with rival" as merely `off-beat` is too tidy; the lawsuit is a high-profile, current reputational fact reporters will use, not just a crisis-comms inconvenience.
